title: Blush Placement for a Round Face: When the Two-Finger Rule Drags You Down

tables.section: Five years of placement advice, side by side
tables.caption: Round-face blush placement as published, oldest first — seven say higher, one says lower, and the column that disagrees is the useful one
head: Published
Where it appeared
Higher or lower
The placement, and what it warns against
rows: Makeup.com — a beauty-editorial site owned by a large cosmetics group; placement quoted to a named artist

Skip the apples; place the blush below the cheekbone, just above where the contour goes — 'with a lower blush placement, round faces look more sculpted and defined.' Warns against the apples of the cheeks.
Charlotte Tilbury — a luxury cosmetics house

Apply slightly higher on the cheeks; using the outer corners of the eyes as a guideline, sweep onto the tops of the apples of the cheeks for a soft lift. No round-specific warning — the section is framed positively, placement 'slightly higher … without accentuating the natural roundness of the cheeks.'
Higher on the cheekbones, swept diagonally from the apples toward the temples. Warns: 'Avoid applying blush directly on the apples of your cheeks, as this can make your face appear rounder.'
Byrdie — a beauty-editorial site, quoting two named artists
On top of the cheekbone below the temple, slightly above the apples angling up toward the temples — 'a vertical pull that visually slims and sculpts.' Warns against adding roundness.

Slightly higher than the apples, swept up toward the temples to elongate; two fingers under the eye from the outer corner set the inner limit. Concedes 'the apples aren't always the best spot for everyone' and warns that blush placed too low 'can emphasise sagging or make features appear to droop.'
Diagonally from the temples toward the top of the cheekbones, keeping most of the colour high. Warns: 'avoid the centre of the cheeks.'

High on the cheekbones, diffused toward the temples for vertical lift; above the nostril line; a cool or neutral rose in a light-to-medium depth. Warns against extending below the nostril line and against letting the colour sit as a hard edge.
Higher on the cheekbones, blended up toward the temples. Warns: 'Avoid the apples of the cheeks to prevent a fuller look.'
tables.footnote: Five of these dates were read off the rendered page: Charlotte Tilbury prints '23rd June 2025', Napoleon Perdis 'October 06, 2025', Smytten 'Published Date - 12 February 2026', Laura Mercier 'March 26, 2026' and Patrick Ta 'Jul 8, 2026'. Two were read out of structured metadata rather than a printed dateline, and they are the two to be careful with: Makeup.com carries datePublished 2021-05-21 and dateModified 2025-07-22, so the oldest end of the span is a metadata field and the page has been revised since; Byrdie carries datePublished 2025-12-04. No7 prints no date anywhere, in the body or in its metadata, so its row is undated and its place in the order is not firm. One further check, because two of these pages could have been the same source counted twice: the round-face paragraph in the Charlotte Tilbury row also appears, lightly reworded, on a Cosmopolitan magazine page quoting the same makeup artist — the shared fingerprint is the clause 'sweep … onto the tops of the cheekbones to create a soft lift effect that helps bring structure to the face.' They are one origin, not two, so that magazine page is deliberately not counted as a separate row; the eight above are eight distinct sources. The names are here so each row can be checked by somebody who is not us. No links are given to any of them.
